Prince '''Alexander Alexeevich Kropotkin''' ({{langx|ru|Алекса́ндр Алексе́евич Кропо́ткин}}, 1841–1886) was a Russian mathematician and populariser of astronomy, and was the brother of the anarchist theorist [[Peter Kropotkin|Pyotr Alexeevich Kropotkin]].

==Biography==

Alexander Kropotkin was born in 1841 into the family of Major General Alexei Petrovich Kropotkin (1805–1871).<ref name="RU">{{cite journal |title=Исторический вестник. Историко-литературный журнал. Том XXV |trans-title=Historical Bulletin. Historical and literary journal. Volume XXVI |url=https://runivers.ru/bookreader/book483262/#page/252/mode/1up |journal=Historical Bulletin- Runivers.ru |access-date=2021-07-25 |page=247 |date=1886 |quote=Vol XXVI}}</ref>

He was the second youngest boy of four children. His brother Pyotr was a year younger, and another brother, Nicholas, and a sister, Helen, were older.<ref name="Atlantic"/> His father was a royal officer who owned serfs in three provinces and whose family descended from the [[Prince of Smolensk|princes of Smolensk]].<ref>Osofsky 1979, pp. 22–23.</ref><ref name="PK8">{{cite web |title=Petr Alekseevich Kropotkin (1842-1921) {{!}} Embryo Project Encyclopedia |url=https://embryo.asu.edu/pages/petr-alekseevich-kropotkin-1842-1921 |website=embryo.asu.edu |date=1 June 2015 |access-date=17 March 2025 |language=en}}</ref> His mother, Ekatarina Sulima, was the daughter of General [[Nikolai Sulima]] and a descendant of a Zaporozhian Cossack leader. 

His mother died of tuberculosis when he was about six and a half years of age.<ref>Osofsky 1979, p. 23</ref> Kropotkin's father remarried two years later, to Yelizaveta Mar'kovna Korandino.<ref name="Spartacus">{{cite web |title=Alexander Kropotkin |url=https://spartacus-educational.com/Alexander_Kropotkin.htm |website=Spartacus Educational |access-date=17 March 2025}}</ref> The stepmother was indifferent towards the Kropotkin children and had a streak of jealous vindictiveness, going through great lengths to remove the memory of Kropotkin's mother.<ref>Osofsky 1979, p. 24</ref>

Alexander Kropotkin published articles on astronomy and celestial mechanics in "[[Russkoye Bogatstvo]]" and in specialized French and English journals, and was a journalist who wrote for the Siberian press.<ref name="RU"/>

He became radicalised as a follower of [[Pyotr Lavrov]].<ref name="PK33">Osofsky 1979, p. 35</ref>

On his return from Europe to Russia in 1876, he was arrested by the police. The conclusion of the head of the Third Section on his case stated that he was not guilty as provided for by the law on punishment for political crimes, but he had demonstrated an "extremely harmful" way of thinking, and therefore his case was resolved not by a judicial but by an administrative procedure. He was accused of helping his brother Peter, who had escaped from the [[Peter and Paul Fortress]] and was living abroad, for which he was exiled to [[Tomsk Oblast]] until 3 September 1886.{{which calendar|date=March 2025}} ({{OldStyleDate|29 August|1886|9 September}} in another source.<ref name="Spartacus"/>) He participated in the publication of the newspaper "Sibirsky Vestnik" ("''Siberian Herald''").<ref name="RU"/>

Before the end of his exile, his wife and three young children were sent to relatives in [[Kharkov Oblast]], where he intended to go from [[Siberia]]. However, on {{OldStyleDate|6 August|1886|25 July}}, at about nine o'clock in the evening,<ref>St. Petersburg Eastern Review, reported in Spartacus reference.</ref> Kropotkin shot himself with a revolver. One source states that although "after the departure of his family, he began to lead an irregular life, he had no motive to take his own life"<ref name="RU"/> -however, another source suggests that a refusal of compassionate prison leave to visit one of his children, reported to be dying, may have been a factor.<ref name="Atlantic">{{cite web |last1=Ely |first1=Robert Erskine |title=Prince Kropotkin |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/1898/09/prince-kropotkin/636407/ |website=The Atlantic |access-date=17 March 2025 |language=en |date=1 September 1898}}</ref>

Afterwards, Alexander Kropotkin's ailing widow (who was left with three small children to care for) was nursed back to health by [[Sophie Kropotkin]], her sister-in-law, in London.<ref name="SK38">{{cite book |last1=Woodcock |first1=George |last2=Avakumović |first2=Ivan |title=Peter Kropotkin, from prince to rebell |date=1990 |publisher=Black Rose Books |location=Montréal |isbn=0-921689-60-8 |page=211}}</ref>

==Family and children==
* Wife — Vera ('Faith') Sevastyanovna Berynda-Tchaikovsky (1849–1935).<ref>{{cite web |title=Faith Sevastyanovna Berynda-Tchaikovsky - Ancestry® |url=https://www.ancestry.com.au/genealogy/records/faith-sevastyanovna-berynda-tchaikovsky-24-2lhmggv?geo_a=r&geo_s=au&geo_t=au&geo_v=2.0.0&o_iid=41020&o_lid=41020&o_sch=Web+Property |website=www.ancestry.com.au |access-date=17 March 2025 |language=en-AU}}</ref>
* Son — Nikolai Alexandrovich Kropotkin (1878–1949).<ref>{{cite web |title=My Memories of Peter Kropotkin by Nikolai A |url=https://docslib.org/doc/2167449/my-memories-of-peter-kropotkin-by-nikolai-a |website=Docslib |access-date=17 March 2025 |language=en}}</ref>
* Grandson — [[Pyotr Nikolaevich Kropotkin]] (1910–1996).
